newsitem.title: USA: U.S. mortgage lenders use varied rate swing hedges.
newsitem.headline: U.S. mortgage lenders use varied rate swing hedges.

text.p: To ride out sharp declines in interest rates which can erode the value of a mortgage banker's loan servicing portfolio, lenders have come to rely on a variety of financial instruments.

Consumers have become increasingly savvy about refinancing to take advantage of low interest rate environments, so lenders are also looking to ensure that if borrowers refinance, they do so with their existing mortgage company.

Until last Friday, when the Treasury market sold off sharply and rates surged, there were widespread expectations of a mini-refinancing wave. But while higher rates have erased the possibility of a major refinancing wave, market observers contended that some refinancing activity will occur.

According to the Mortgage Bankers Association of America (MBA), 31.4 percent of mortgage banking activity in the week ended July 25 was refinance related. The MBA's refinancing index rose 9.8 percent from the prior week to 595.9.

According to David Lereah, chief economist at the MBA, refinancings may pick up in the week ended August 1 because borrowing costs were low earlier that week. The survey for the week ended August 1 will be released on Thursday.

Ahead of last Friday's rate rise, many fixed-rate loans in excess of 8.0 percent or 8.5 percent were refinanceable, said Mike Heid, executive vice president of Norwest Mortgage Inc's loan servicing division.

"We have not seen a huge surge in refinancings yet and probably won't until rates go lower," said Jeff Speakes, managing director of risk management at Pasadena, California-based Countrywide Credit Industries.

A Treasury 10-year note yield drop to 6.0 percent could have sparked refinancing in loans originated in the last year or year-and-a-half, he said. The rate was 6.23 percent Tuesday, having briefly hit 6.00 percent last Thursday.
"In late 1995 and in early 1996, the 10-year note was lower than 5.75 percent and that was the last mini-refinancing wave," recalled Speakes.

Meanwhile, refinancings among so-called B and C credit borrowers -- that is lesser quality borrowers -- have risen over the last three months, said David Olson, a partner at Columbia, Maryland-based Wholesale Access.
"This could be competition from other lenders for customers," Olson said, noting that lenders often have to match rates offered by competitors.

Heid said that while there was a modest rise in refinancings as borrowers prepaid, some of that was a typical seasonal increase. "We still think more of the activity is seasonal as opposed to refinance driven," said Heid.

"Home mortgage interest rates have to dip below 7.0 percent to have a real active refinance market," he said, noting that servicers with an 8.50 percent interest rate portfolio were seeing heightened prepayments. Norwest's servicing portfolio has a lower average rate of 7.78 percent.
Still, mortgage bankers remained vigilant about protecting against wide rate swings. "We have an ongoing hedging program. You need to manage all interest rate cycles," said Heid.
The hedging tools used include interest rate options, options on futures contracts or over-the-counter options as well as interest rate floors.

Countrywide's Speakes said his firm has used derivatives such as principal-only securities (POs), which are bonds created deliberately to pay only principal. POs are purchased at a discount, and investors make their money when loans are prepaid because the bonds are paid at par.

A firm's interest rate exposure depends on the extent that it originates or services loans. A company that relies heavily on originations may be more vulnerable to higher rates, while a firm with a large servicing portfolio tends to be more vulnerable to low rate environments.

If borrowers do decide to refinance, lenders hope they will stay with their current mortgage lender. So, the effect of financial tools in hedging portfolio losses is bolstered by campaigns to retain borrowers during refinancings.
"We certainly want to maintain relationships with our customers. We hope customers come back," said Speakes.
